Distributed systems use WAL for consensus (Raft, Multi-Paxos). Kafka uses log-structured storage exclusively. WAL enables point-in-time recovery by replaying to specific timestamps. Replicas consume WAL for synchronization. Consider log compaction to remove obsolete entries while preserving latest state.

sections.title: Radical Microservices Decomposition
sections.content: Zalando, Europe's largest online fashion retailer, operates one of the most aggressive microservices architectures with over 1,500 independently deployable services. The decomposition followed domain-driven design with bounded contexts around business capabilities: catalog (product information), inventory (stock levels), pricing (dynamic pricing), cart (shopping basket), checkout (payment processing), fulfillment (order processing), and customer (profiles and preferences). Each team owns multiple services end-to-end including development, deployment, and operations. Services communicate exclusively via REST APIs or event streams—no shared databases. This autonomy enables fast development (teams deploy independently 50+ times per day) but introduces distributed system challenges. Service discovery uses Kubernetes DNS, API gateway handles external traffic routing, and circuit breakers prevent cascading failures. The architecture scales to handle 100 million visits per month and 50,000 orders per day.

sections.title: Skipper API Gateway
sections.content: Zalando built Skipper, an HTTP router and API gateway handling all external and internal traffic. Skipper runs as Kubernetes pods (100+ instances) behind AWS Network Load Balancers, processing over 200,000 requests per second at peak. Routing rules are defined in Git and deployed continuously—when a team updates their service's routing configuration, the change propagates to all Skipper instances within 30 seconds via Kubernetes ConfigMaps. Skipper provides sophisticated routing capabilities: weighted traffic splitting for blue-green deployments, shadow traffic copying to test new versions, rate limiting per client, authentication via OAuth2, request/response transformation, and automatic retries with exponential backoff. The gateway implements health checks and circuit breakers—if a backend service's error rate exceeds 10%, Skipper automatically stops routing traffic and returns cached responses or fallback data. Skipper's design is stateless (routing rules are config, no database), enabling horizontal scaling and fast rollouts. The team open-sourced Skipper, and it's used by other large-scale European tech companies.

sections.title: Nakadi Event Streaming Platform
sections.content: Zalando built Nakadi, an event streaming platform that provides a REST API over Apache Kafka. Nakadi abstracts Kafka's complexity, allowing teams to publish and consume events via simple HTTP requests without learning Kafka clients, ZooKeeper, or consumer group management. Events follow a standard schema (JSON with event type, metadata, and payload) enforced by JSON Schema validation. Event types are versioned with compatibility rules ensuring backward compatibility. For example, the 'order.placed' event type defines fields like order_id, customer_id, and items. Consumers subscribe via Server-Sent Events (SSE), receiving a stream of events over long-lived HTTP connections. Nakadi handles Kafka consumer group management, offset tracking, and rebalancing transparently. The platform processes over 1 billion events per day across 500+ event types. Zalando uses events for cross-service communication (publish-subscribe), data pipeline ingestion, and audit logging. The event-driven architecture enables loose coupling—services don't need to know about downstream consumers, they just publish events and move on.

sections.title: Database Per Service Pattern
sections.content: Zalando enforces database-per-service pattern where each microservice owns its database schema and other services cannot directly access it. This provides loose coupling and independent scaling but introduces challenges for cross-service queries. For example, displaying order history with product details requires joining order data (order service database) with product data (catalog service database). Zalando solves this through several patterns: API composition (order service calls catalog service API to fetch product details), data replication (catalog service publishes product update events, order service consumes and maintains a local denormalized copy), and CQRS (separate read models optimized for queries, updated via events). Most services use PostgreSQL for primary storage due to strong consistency, ACID guarantees, and powerful query capabilities. Some services use Redis for caching, Elasticsearch for search, and S3 for blob storage. The database-per-service pattern enables teams to choose appropriate data stores and schema designs for their domain without coordination, though it requires careful event-driven integration.

documents.title: Zero Trust Architecture: Security for Modern Infrastructure

sections.content: Zero trust architecture eliminates implicit trust, requiring verification for every access attempt regardless of network location. Traditional perimeter security assumes internal network traffic is trustworthy, creating vulnerabilities when perimeters are breached. Zero trust replaces network location-based trust with identity-based verification, authenticating and authorizing every request. The principle of least privilege grants minimum necessary access, reducing blast radius from compromised credentials. Micro-segmentation isolates resources, preventing lateral movement by attackers. Continuous verification monitors ongoing sessions for anomalous behavior, revoking access when risk increases. Assume breach mentality treats internal and external threats equivalently, implementing detective and responsive controls. Zero trust enables cloud adoption, remote work, and third-party integrations without expanding attack surface. Implementation requires coordinating identity, device, network, and application security controls into cohesive architecture.
sections.title: Zero Trust Principles and Philosophy

sections.content: Identity forms the new security perimeter in zero trust architecture. Centralized identity providers (IdP) like Okta, Azure AD, or Google Workspace serve as trust anchors, authenticating users and devices. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) strengthens authentication beyond passwords, requiring possession factors (mobile device, hardware token) or biometric factors. Risk-based authentication adjusts requirements based on context: IP address, device posture, time of day, or data sensitivity. Single sign-on (SSO) centralizes authentication, simplifying user experience while enabling consistent security policy enforcement. Just-in-time access grants temporary permissions for specific tasks, reducing standing privileges. Privileged access management (PAM) protects administrative credentials with vaulting, session recording, and approval workflows. Service accounts use short-lived credentials or workload identity, avoiding static secrets. Identity governance ensures access reviews, certification campaigns, and automated deprovisioning of terminated users.
sections.title: Identity and Access Management

sections.content: Zero trust network access (ZTNA) replaces VPNs with identity-aware proxies, authenticating before granting network access. Software-defined perimeters (SDP) hide infrastructure from untrusted networks, making resources invisible until identity verification succeeds. Service meshes like Istio or Linkerd enforce zero trust for microservices, requiring mutual TLS between all services. Network segmentation divides infrastructure into security zones with explicit inter-zone policies. East-west traffic inspection monitors lateral movement between services, detecting and blocking attacks. DNS-based security identifies command-and-control traffic or data exfiltration attempts through anomalous DNS queries. Next-generation firewalls (NGFW) inspect traffic at application layer, enforcing policies based on application identity rather than IP addresses and ports. Cloud security groups implement micro-segmentation with instance-level firewall rules. Intent-based networking automatically configures network controls from declarative security policies, reducing configuration errors.
sections.title: Network Security and Segmentation

sections.content: Implementing zero trust requires phased approach, starting with highest-value assets. Begin with identity foundation: deploy IdP, enable SSO, and require MFA. Inventory assets and data flows to understand current state and dependencies. Deploy zero trust network access solutions like Zscaler Private Access, Cloudflare Access, or Tailscale for remote access. Implement service mesh for microservices communication, gradually enforcing mutual TLS. Deploy endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools for device posture verification and threat detection. Use cloud access security brokers (CASB) for visibility and control over SaaS applications. Implement data loss prevention (DLP) to detect and prevent sensitive data exfiltration. Deploy security information and event management (SIEM) for centralized logging and correlation. Use infrastructure as code for consistent, auditable security control deployment. Measure progress with metrics like percentage of traffic encrypted, MFA adoption rate, and mean time to detect threats.
sections.title: Implementation Strategies and Tools
Introduction: Motivation for Retrieval-Augmented Forecasting
sections.content: RAFT (Retrieval Augmented Time Series Forecasting) proposes a method that enhances time series forecasting by retrieving similar historical patterns from training data. Real-world time series exhibit complex, non-stationary patterns with varying periods that lack temporal correlation. Rather than forcing models to memorize all patterns, RAFT provides retrieved historical information explicitly at inference time. By directly utilizing retrieved information, useful patterns become explicitly available instead of relying solely on learned model weights. This retrieval-augmented approach augments model capacity by providing external information about historical patterns, similar to how RAG enhances LLMs with external knowledge.

sections.title: Related Work: Deep Learning and Retrieval for Time Series
sections.content: The paper reviews CNN, RNN, and Transformer-based approaches for time series forecasting including Informer, AutoFormer, and FedFormer. Recent lightweight models like DLinear, TiDE, and TimeMixer demonstrate that simple architectures with proper inductive biases can match complex models. RAG approaches from NLP retrieve relevant documents to supplement LLM knowledge. RAFT extends this retrieval concept to single time-series forecasting, unlike prior work that retrieves across multiple time-series entities. This represents a novel application of retrieval-augmented generation principles to temporal prediction tasks.

sections.title: Retrieval Module Architecture: Patches, Similarity, and Aggregation
sections.content: The retrieval module operates through several key steps: (1) Patch Creation - extract key patches from the training dataset using sliding windows with stride=1, creating patches of size L for lookback. (2) Value Patches - identify corresponding value patches of size F (forecast horizon) that follow each key patch. (3) Offset Normalization - subtract the final timestep value to focus on pattern shape rather than scale, computed as x_hat = x^t - x^L. (4) Similarity Calculation - use Pearson correlation to compute similarity between query and all key patches: rho_i = s(x_hat, k_hat_i). Pearson correlation outperforms cosine similarity and L2 distance. (5) Top-m Retrieval - select indices with highest similarity values. (6) Weighted Aggregation - calculate softmax weights and aggregate: v_tilde = sum(w_i * v_hat_i). This pre-computed retrieval enables O(N^2) offline complexity with minimal inference overhead.

sections.title: Forecast with Multi-Period Retrieval Module
sections.content: For single period forecasting: y_hat = h(f(x_hat) + g(v_tilde)) where f, g, h are linear projections and + denotes concatenation. For multiple periods, RAFT uses multi-periodicity by downsampling with periods {1, 2, 4}: (1) Downsample all patches via average pooling for each period p. (2) Apply retrieval module to period-specific data. (3) Project results to uniform dimension via g^(p). (4) Sum across periods: y_hat = h(f(x_hat) + sum_p(g^(p)(v_tilde^(p)))). (5) Restore original scale: y = y_hat^t + x^L. This multi-period design captures both local and global temporal dynamics. The loss function is standard MSE between predicted and actual values.

sections.title: Experiments: Benchmarks, Baselines, and Results
sections.content: RAFT was evaluated on 10 benchmarks including ETT (electricity transformer temperature), Electricity, Exchange Rate, Illness, Solar, Traffic, and Weather datasets. The method was compared against 9 baselines: Autoformer, Informer, Stationary, FedFormer, PatchTST, DLinear, MICN, TimesNet, and TimeMixer. Hyperparameters were tuned via grid search: learning rate (1e-5 to 0.05), lookback window L ({96, 192, 336, 720}), number of retrievals m ({1, 5, 10, 20}), temperature tau (0.1), and periods ({1, 2, 4}). RAFT achieved an average win ratio of 86% across benchmarks, consistently outperforming baselines on both MSE and MAE metrics across different forecast horizons.

sections.title: Discussions: When Retrieval Helps Most
sections.content: The paper provides analysis of when retrieval-augmented forecasting is most effective: (1) Better Retrieval leads to Better Performance - positive correlation (0.60 Spearman) between key similarity and value similarity, and negative correlation (-0.54) between value similarity and MSE. (2) Helpful for Rare Patterns - synthetic experiments with autoregressive models demonstrate retrieval improves performance 9.2-14.7% more when patterns occur rarely, as models struggle to memorize infrequent behaviors. (3) Helpful for Temporally Uncorrelated Patterns - random-walk synthetic experiments show larger gains (16.0-31.5% MSE reduction) compared to autoregressive patterns, indicating retrieval excels when temporal correlation is weak. (4) Applicable to Transformers - adding the retrieval module to AutoFormer improves performance, demonstrating broader applicability beyond MLP architectures. This reduces learning burden for complex, non-correlated patterns while maintaining computational efficiency.

documents.title: Context Engineering for AI Agents: Lessons from Building Manus

sections.title: Design Around the KV-Cache
sections.content: The KV-cache is the true context of LLMs - not the text itself. Avoid patterns that invalidate cache: don't remove text, don't modify existing content, don't dynamically reorder items. Manus moves away from dynamic few-shot example selection based on query similarity because this makes prefix unstable and invalidates cache. Instead use stable prefixes and append-only context updates. Cache invalidation costs both latency and money (no prompt cache discounts). Agents require iterative steps and stability of earlier portions lets you avoid regenerating from scratch. Design context like an append-only log for optimal KV-cache utilization.

sections.title: Mask, Don't Remove: Tool Management with State Machines
sections.content: Instead of dynamically adding/removing tools from context, keep all tools in context and use logits masking to prevent selection of currently invalid tools. This maintains stable token positions (preserving KV-cache) while still constraining behavior. Manus uses a state machine where current state determines which tools are masked via logit bias. This is more efficient than regenerating context when tool availability changes. The approach works with function calling by masking tokens that would select invalid tools. State machine transitions control tool availability without context modification.

sections.title: Use the File System as Context
sections.content: For long tasks, Manus delegates memory to the file system rather than keeping everything in context. Agents create, read, and edit files as external memory. This works naturally because modern LLMs are trained extensively on coding tasks and understand file operations. Compressed context (summaries in files) scales better than ever-growing context windows. The file system acts as unlimited external memory while context maintains working memory. This pattern enables handling tasks that would exceed context limits while maintaining coherent state across operations.

sections.title: Manipulate Attention Through Recitation
sections.content: When agents need to 'remember' specific information buried deep in context, have them recite it rather than rely on attention finding it. Attention patterns can miss critical details in long contexts. By having the agent explicitly output important information before using it, you ensure the relevant details are in recent context with high attention weights. This 'recitation' technique makes retrieval from context more reliable. Particularly useful when critical information was established early in a long conversation but needed much later.

sections.title: Keep the Wrong Stuff: Error Preservation for Learning
sections.content: Manus intentionally preserves error messages, failed attempts, and corrections in context. This teaches the model what not to do and prevents repetition of mistakes. When errors are removed, the model loses signal about what approaches failed. The context becomes a learning trace showing both failures and successes. This is counterintuitive (removing failures seems cleaner) but empirically improves agent performance. Errors in context serve as negative examples during inference, helping the model avoid similar mistakes.

sections.title: Avoid Pattern Rigidity: Few-Shot Example Pitfalls
sections.content: Few-shot examples can cause harmful pattern-following where agents mimic example structure too rigidly. Manus found that providing examples led to agents replicating superficial patterns rather than understanding underlying principles. Zero-shot with clear instructions often produces more flexible, appropriate behavior. If examples are necessary, use diverse examples that demonstrate variation rather than a single pattern. This prevents the 'template copying' failure mode where agents follow example format even when inappropriate for the current task.
